Gamers Nexus, in your video you noted that SLI isn't useful in tile based rendering. SLI can be used in tile based rendering to allow memory pooling between GPUs. So with 2x3090 your total VRAM will be 48GB (2x24GB). However, I believe the developer needs to add support for memory pooling.

At least this has been my impression based on patches made to Blender's Cycles rendering engine.

Initial memory pooling patch for Cycles: https://developer.blender.org/D7426

Final commit for Cycles: https://developer.blender.org/rB9f7d84b656fbb56966620ecc249ce5bc7089a1d1

In theory the PCIe bus could be used for memory pooling, but using the SLI bridge alleviates load on the PCIe bus.

Either way. Thanks for making these informative videos.

text:
With respect to the PCIe Gen 4 comments, is it really just the 2-3% difference? It's been stated (and tested) that a single 3080 installed in a single Gen 3 x16 slot loses only a couple of percentage points worth of performance in certain workloads compared the same card installed into a PCIe Gen 4 x16 slot. But in this scenario, are both of the PCIe slots in the motherboard used here capable of PCIe Gen 3 x16 if both are populated? I wasn't aware of any Z490 boards which can operate more than one slot at Gen 3 x16, most boards will knock both slots down to Gen 3 x8. It would be the same on most X570 boards, which should run both slots at Gen 4 x8. With this in mind, it isn't really fair to say that a pair of 3090's in an Intel board which has both cards at Gen 3 x8, is comparable to an X570 board that would in theory have both slots at Gen 4 x8. The bandwidth difference should matter somewhere now that we're talking about running 3090's at Gen 3 x8 speeds, right?

PCIe Gen 3 most likely scenario of 1 x Gen 3 x8 + 1 x Gen 3 x8 = 7.87GB/s + 7.87GB/s = 15.75GB/a
PCIe Gen 4 most likely scenario of 1 x Gen 4 x8 + 1 x Gen 4 x8 = 15.75GB/s +15.75GB/s = 31.5GB/s

I'd like to see this tested in a high-end X570 or TRX board to see if we get similar results. It's possible that with so much of the work happening within the GPU card themselves and not having to go back and forth with the CPU/memory/SSD, being dropped to Gen 3 x8 isn't introducing a bottleneck. I'd still like to know if the 3090, or dual 3090's benefit from moving to Gen 4 slots with benchmarks like Port Royal or Time Spy.

text:
With respect to the PCIe Gen 4 comments, is it really just the 2-3% difference? It's been stated (and tested) that a single 3080 installed in a single Gen 3 x16 slot loses only a couple of percentage points worth of performance in certain workloads compared the same card installed into a PCIe Gen 4 x16 slot. But in this scenario, are both of the PCIe slots in the motherboard used here capable of PCIe Gen 3 x16 if both are populated? I wasn't aware of any Z490 boards which can operate more than one slot at Gen 3 x16, most boards will knock both slots down to Gen 3 x8. It would be the same on most X570 boards, which should run both slots at Gen 4 x8. With this in mind, it isn't really fair to say that a pair of 3090's in an Intel board which has both cards at Gen 3 x8, is comparable to an X570 board that would in theory have both slots at Gen 4 x8. The bandwidth difference should matter somewhere now that we're talking about running 3090's at Gen 3 x8 speeds, right?

PCIe Gen 3 most likely scenario of 1 x Gen 3 x8 + 1 x Gen 3 x8 = 7.87GB/s + 7.87GB/s = 15.75GB/a
PCIe Gen 4 most likely scenario of 1 x Gen 4 x8 + 1 x Gen 4 x8 = 15.75GB/s +15.75GB/s = 31.5GB/s

I'd like to see this tested in a high-end X570 or TRX board to see if we get similar results. It's possible that with so much of the work happening within the GPU card themselves and not having to go back and forth with the CPU/memory/SSD, being dropped to Gen 3 x8 isn't introducing a bottleneck. I'd still like to know if the 3090, or dual 3090's benefit from moving to Gen 4 slots with benchmarks like Port Royal or Time Spy.

text:
Disclaimer: I agree with you that SLI is officially dead with this release.
That being said, two things Steve:
1. Why would you show Hitman 2 and not Hitman 1 when H1 was the game on the list supported?
2. I understand you catering to your audience with rhetorics that +50% performance boost for 100% price increase is not worth it but here is the thing -  most of the high end things work like that in real life. You pay certain amount of money for up to 80-90% but if you want that couple % more, the price goes up exponentially. The value has never been there, only the possibility to achieve that.

If this "POOR" +50-60% scaling makes it possible to push a title past 60FPS or up to 120FPS in resolutions 4k+ then it is absolutely irrelevant that it's "only" 50-60% increase for a 100% price increase because there is no way for an individual to get got those numbers without it. Since Turing you can't even say "just buy a better card instead of 2x weaker ones" - what about the fact that you already have top of the line card? Where are you supposed to get more performance from?

This is what many people failed to understand while arguing about SLI in previous releases. It's not about getting 100% performance increase with 100% cost increase, it's about pushing the FPS higher than it is possible in the current generation. In that sense, scaling in the line of 50-60% is actually quite nice and worth it to many people - if it were consistent across the board with all games.

This is why the death of SLI is a tragedy. It may not be for everyone but the rich people but technology should strive to push past the limits. Right now NVIDIA is saying that a single 3090 is the best one could do, period. It would be nice to be able consistently achieve even more.

author: @weavercs4014

text:
@jayhill2193  I'd guess the modern hourglass shape of nVidia SLI bridges minimises airflow blockage between adjacent cards. In the Good Old Days of 50W TDP graphics cards being top-of-the-range then a 5cm-wide ribbon connecting two GPUs wouldn't be much of a hassle, now if you're running two or more smoking hot room heaters racked next to each other they need every airflow and cooling mitigation they can come up with -- see the 3090 FE's exotic cooling architecture to cope with 300W plus of waste heat.

The other advantage of a rigid SLI bridge is that it offers some structural rigidity between big heavy cards meaning the strain on the PCIe slots they're plugged into is spread out somewhat.
